title: Equilibrium and Elasticity
bigQuestion: If buyers and sellers each want their own price, how does a market settle on one, and why do some prices move so much more than others?

story.title: Face Value: $75. Resale: $300.
story.kicker: Eighteen thousand seats, a hundred thousand fans, and a price on the ticket that nobody actually paid.
paragraphs: The tour announcement came on a Tuesday. A singer who had sold out arenas across the country would play one night at the big arena on Chicago's Near West Side. Tickets would go on sale Friday at 10 a.m. Face value for most seats: $75. Jada, a junior at a high school in Cicero, set three alarms. She had been waiting two years for this.

At 9:58 Friday morning she was in the online waiting room with a number over 90,000 in front of her. The arena holds about 18,000 for a concert. By 10:09 the screen said every seat was gone. Jada refreshed. Same message. She had not even gotten to the page where you pick a section. Neither had most of the people in line.

By noon the same seats were on a resale site. Upper level: $220. Lower level: $340. Floor: $900 and up. The tickets had not changed. The concert had not changed. Only the price had, and it had quadrupled in two hours. Jada's first reaction was that someone was cheating. Her second reaction, after she calmed down, was a question: if people will pay $300, why did the singer charge $75 in the first place?

Her economics teacher put two numbers on the board. Seats: 18,000, and that number cannot go up no matter what the price is. Fans who want a ticket at $75: maybe 60,000. When the number people want is bigger than the number that exists, something besides price has to decide who gets one. On Friday it was speed and luck. By noon it was money again, on a different website.

This chapter is about that meeting point between buyers and sellers, and what happens when the price is not allowed to reach it. It is also about a second question hidden in the story: why fans would pay four times face value for a concert but would never pay four times the usual price for a gallon of milk. Both answers come from the same two curves you built in the last chapter.
story.think: The singer could have charged $250 and probably still sold every seat. List two reasons an artist might choose $75 anyway. Who gains and who loses from that choice?

lessons.title: Finding the Meeting Point
lessons.mainIdea: Equilibrium is the one price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, and a market tends to move toward it.
reading: Put a demand schedule and a supply schedule side by side and something jumps out. Consider tomatoes at a Saturday farmers market, priced per pound. At $1, buyers want 500 pounds but sellers bring only 100. At $2, buyers want 400 and sellers bring 200. At $3, buyers want 300 and sellers bring 300. At $4, buyers want 200 and sellers bring 400. At $5, buyers want 100 and sellers bring 500. Only one row matches: $3, where 300 pounds are wanted and 300 are offered.

That price is the *equilibrium price*, and 300 pounds is the *equilibrium quantity*. Equilibrium is a word borrowed from physics. It means a resting point, a place where the forces balance. At $3 every buyer who is willing to pay finds a seller, and every seller who is willing to sell finds a buyer. No one is left holding tomatoes and no one goes home empty-handed who was willing to pay the going price.

A market has no manager who sets this price. It emerges. If sellers try $5, they will have 400 unsold pounds at the end of the day and will cut prices. If they try $1, they will sell out by 9 a.m. and notice they could have charged more. Both mistakes push the price back toward $3. Economists call this the *market-clearing price*, because at $3 the market clears: what is brought is what is bought.

The economist Alfred Marshall, writing in 1890, compared demand and supply to the two blades of a pair of scissors. Asking whether the buyers or the sellers set the price is like asking which blade does the cutting. Both do, together. Any change on either side moves the point where the blades cross. The rest of this chapter follows those changes.

words.d: the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
the amount bought and sold at the equilibrium price
another name for the equilibrium price; everything brought to market is bought

look.title: The Two Blades
look.text: Marshall argued that it is pointless to ask whether value is set by what buyers are willing to pay or by what it costs to produce a good. That is like asking whether the top blade or the bottom blade of a pair of scissors cuts the paper. Both must move together.
look.prompt: Using the tomato table, explain in your own words why neither buyers alone nor sellers alone can set the $3 price.

check.q: In the tomato market, what is the equilibrium price?
check.why: At $3 quantity demanded (300) equals quantity supplied (300). No other row matches.

check.q: What does it mean that a market clears at the equilibrium price?
choices: All buyers get a tomato for free
Everything brought to market is bought, with no leftover and no one turned away who will pay
The government has approved the price
check.why: At equilibrium the quantity offered equals the quantity wanted, so nothing is left over and nothing is short.

check.q: If sellers set the tomato price at $5, what will they notice, and what will they do?
choices: They sell out fast and raise the price
Buyers and sellers are both satisfied
They have 400 unsold pounds and cut the price
Buyers bring more money next week
check.why: At $5 supply is 500 and demand is 100. The 400 leftover pounds push sellers to lower the price toward $3.

lessons.title: Shortage: Price Too Low
lessons.mainIdea: When the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer, and the shortage pushes the price up.
reading: Suppose the tomato sellers, for whatever reason, price at $2. Buyers want 400 pounds. Sellers brought 200. The gap, 400 minus 200, is a *shortage* of 200 pounds. A shortage is the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a particular price. It is not the same as scarcity, which is always true of everything. A shortage exists only at a price below equilibrium, and it disappears when the price rises.

What happens next in a real market? Some buyers who really want tomatoes offer more. A seller with a short line and an eager crowd raises the sign to $2.50. As the price climbs, two things happen at once. Some buyers drop out, so quantity demanded falls from 400 toward 300. Sellers bring more from the truck, so quantity supplied rises from 200 toward 300. At $3 the gap is gone. The shortage itself was the pressure that fixed it.

While the shortage lasts, the market needs another way to decide who gets the tomatoes. Usually it is first come, first served: a line. It can also be luck, connections with the seller, or a limit of two per customer. Economists call this *non-price rationing*. It is what Jada ran into on the ticket site. At $75 there were far more buyers than seats, so speed and luck did the choosing, not price.

Back at the arena, the shortage was enormous. Sixty thousand fans wanted a seat at $75 and 18,000 seats existed. The shortage was 42,000. The resale site was where the price finally rose toward equilibrium and buyers who valued the seat most, or had the most money, got them. Whether that outcome is fair is a real argument. That it happened is simply what shortages do.

words.d: at a given price, the amount by which quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied
deciding who gets a good by lines, luck, limits or connections instead of by price
the basic fact that wants exceed resources; it is always true, unlike a shortage

look.title: The $75 Ticket
look.text: The arena has 18,000 seats. At a face price of $75, about 60,000 fans want a ticket. At $150, about 35,000 want one. At $250, about 18,000 want one. At $400, about 9,000 want one. The artist sets the price at $75 and every ticket sells out in nine minutes.
look.prompt: How big is the shortage at $75? At $150? What price would clear the market? Who ends up with tickets at $75, and who ends up with them once resale is allowed?

check.q: At $2, buyers want 400 pounds of tomatoes and sellers bring 200. What is the shortage?
check.why: Shortage equals quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 400 minus 200 equals 200 pounds.

check.q: How does a shortage fix itself in a free market?
choices: The price rises, so quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises until they meet
Sellers give away the extra goods
The price falls until all buyers are served
check.why: A shortage pushes the price up. The higher price both discourages some buyers and brings more supply.

check.q: Which is an example of non-price rationing?
choices: Raising the price until the line disappears
Selling tickets first come, first served until they run out
Lowering the price to sell more
Adding more seats to the arena
check.why: First come, first served uses time and luck, not price, to decide who gets the good.

lessons.title: Surplus: Price Too High
lessons.mainIdea: When the price is above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, and the surplus pushes the price down.
reading: Now flip it. Sellers price tomatoes at $4. Buyers want only 200 pounds, but sellers brought 400. The extra 200 pounds is a *surplus*: the amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a particular price. Surplus is the mirror image of shortage. It appears only when the price is above equilibrium, and it goes away when the price falls.

Sellers do not enjoy watching tomatoes rot. One seller marks down to $3.50 to move product. Others follow. As the price falls, quantity demanded rises from 200 toward 300, and some sellers decide not to bring as much next week, so quantity supplied falls from 400 toward 300. The price settles at $3 and the surplus is gone. Clearance racks, end-of-season sales and "buy one get one" deals are all surplus at work.

A surplus is also what unsold *inventory* looks like on a company's books. When a video game console sits on shelves for months, the retailer has priced above what buyers will pay at that quantity. When it cuts the price, it is not being generous. It is moving toward equilibrium. When you see a big markdown, ask which side of the market misjudged, and by how much.

Here is the whole picture in one line. Below equilibrium, shortage, price rises. Above equilibrium, surplus, price falls. At equilibrium, neither, price stays. In a market where the price is free to move, it keeps getting pushed back toward the crossing point. The next chapter looks at what happens when a law stops the price from moving. This chapter stays with prices that can.

words.d: at a given price, the amount by which quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
goods a seller has made or bought but not yet sold
a price cut a seller makes to sell goods that were not selling at the old price

look.title: Tomatoes: Wanted Minus Offered
look.cite: Built from the tomato schedules in this section; a labeled example.
look.prompt: A positive number is a shortage and a negative number is a surplus. At which price is there neither? What does the price do at $4, and why?

check.q: At $4, sellers bring 400 pounds and buyers want 200. This is
check.why: Surplus equals quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 400 minus 200 equals 200 pounds.

check.q: A store has hundreds of unsold winter coats in March and cuts the price by half. In market terms, the store is
choices: removing a surplus by moving toward equilibrium
check.why: Unsold inventory means the price was above equilibrium. The markdown moves the price down toward it.

check.q: Which statement is correct?
choices: Below the equilibrium price there is a shortage and the price tends to rise
Below the equilibrium price there is a surplus and the price tends to fall
Above the equilibrium price there is a shortage
At the equilibrium price there is a small surplus
check.why: Below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer. That shortage pushes the price up.

lessons.title: Demand Shifts: Two Cases
lessons.mainIdea: A rightward demand shift raises both price and quantity; a leftward demand shift lowers both.
reading: Go back to lemonade on Maple Street and give it a supply schedule too. Before the heat wave, buyers wanted 60 cups at 50 cents, 40 at $1, 25 at $1.50 and 15 at $2. Sellers offered 10 at 50 cents, 30 at $1, 45 at $1.50 and 60 at $2. There is no exact match, but the crossing is between $1 and $1.50: at $1 there is a shortage of 10 cups, and at $1.50 a surplus of 20. Say the equilibrium is about $1.15 and about 35 cups.

Now the heat wave shifts demand right. Buyers want 70 cups at $1, 50 at $1.50 and 35 at $2. Supply has not changed. At the old price of about $1.15 there is now a big shortage, so the price rises. At $1.50, buyers want 50 and sellers offer 45, close to a match. The new equilibrium is roughly $1.50 and about 47 cups. Compare the two: price went up and quantity went up. That is the first case, a *rightward shift of demand*.

The second case is the reverse. A cold snap in August shifts demand left. Fewer cups are wanted at every price. At the old price there is a surplus, so the price falls, and at the lower price sellers offer fewer cups. Price down, quantity down. A *leftward shift of demand* lowers both. Whenever price and quantity move in the same direction, suspect that demand shifted.

This is how economists read the news. If a report says a good's price rose and more of it sold, the demand curve moved right. Higher price plus more sales cannot come from a supply shift, because a supply shift pushes price and quantity in opposite directions. The direction of price alone is not enough. You need both numbers to tell which curve moved.

words.d: buyers want more at every price; the equilibrium price and quantity both rise
buyers want less at every price; the equilibrium price and quantity both fall
the price and quantity where the curves cross after one of them has shifted

look.title: Reading the Numbers
look.text: Last year a used-bike shop in Evanston sold about 300 bikes at an average price of $180. This year gas prices rose sharply and many people looked for other ways to commute. The shop sold about 420 bikes at an average price of $230. The shop's costs did not change.
look.prompt: Which curve shifted, and which way? Which shifter caused it? Explain how the two numbers together rule out a supply shift.

check.q: A heat wave shifts lemonade demand right. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
check.why: More demand at every price creates a shortage at the old price. The price rises and sellers respond by offering more.

check.q: Sales of a snack fall and its price falls at the same time. Which is the most likely cause?
check.why: Price and quantity fell together, which only a leftward demand shift produces.

check.q: Why does a rightward demand shift raise quantity sold, if a higher price makes buyers want less?
choices: It does not; quantity always falls when price rises
Because the higher price moves sellers up their supply curve, and they offer more
check.why: The demand curve shifted, so at the new higher price sellers move along their unchanged supply curve and offer more cups.

lessons.title: Supply Shifts: Two Cases
lessons.mainIdea: A leftward supply shift raises price and lowers quantity; a rightward supply shift lowers price and raises quantity.
reading: Now hold demand fixed and move supply. On the third Saturday the price of lemons doubled. Deshawn and Maya offered fewer cups at every price: 18 at $1, 30 at $1.50, 40 at $2 instead of 30, 45 and 60. Demand is the mild-day schedule: 40 at $1, 25 at $1.50, 15 at $2. Before, the equilibrium was about $1.15 and 35 cups. Now at $1.15 there is a shortage, so the price rises. At $1.50 buyers want 25 and sellers offer 30, close. Call the new equilibrium about $1.40 and about 28 cups.

Notice the pattern. Price went up, but quantity went down. That is a *leftward shift of supply*: fewer cups at every price, so the market clears at a higher price and a smaller quantity. Compare it with the heat wave, where price went up and quantity went up. Same direction for price, opposite direction for quantity. That difference is how you tell a demand shift from a supply shift when both raise the price.

The other case is a *rightward shift of supply*. Deshawn's electric juicer lowers his cost, or Leo opens a third stand, and more cups are offered at every price. At the old price there is a surplus, so the price falls, and at the lower price buyers move down their demand curve and buy more. Price down, quantity up. This is what decades of better technology did to the price of a calculator or a flat-screen TV.

Put the four cases in a small table in your head. Demand right: price up, quantity up. Demand left: price down, quantity down. Supply right: price down, quantity up. Supply left: price up, quantity down. A quick way to remember: demand shifts move price and quantity the same way; supply shifts move them opposite ways. Practice on real events until it feels automatic.

words.d: sellers offer less at every price; the equilibrium price rises and quantity falls
sellers offer more at every price; the equilibrium price falls and quantity rises
the four single-curve shifts (demand right or left, supply right or left) and what each does to price and quantity

look.title: Two Stories, One Price Rise
look.text: In the same month, two things happen in Illinois. First, a disease hits egg-laying hens and farms send fewer eggs to market. Second, a national health article makes eggs popular again. Both push the price of eggs up. A grocery chain reports that egg sales in cartons went up.
look.prompt: Which story does the sales number support, and why? If sales had gone down instead, which story would that point to? What would you expect if both happened at once?

check.q: Lemon prices double, shifting lemonade supply left. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
check.why: Fewer cups at every price creates a shortage at the old price. Price rises and buyers cut back along their demand curve.

check.q: Better technology shifts the supply of TVs right. Which pair of results follows?
check.why: More supply at every price creates a surplus at the old price. Price falls and buyers move down their demand curve.

check.q: The price of a good rose and the quantity sold fell. Which curve moved?
check.why: Price and quantity moved in opposite directions, so supply shifted. A higher price means it shifted left.

lessons.title: Both Curves Move at Once
lessons.mainIdea: When demand and supply both shift, one of price or quantity is certain and the other depends on which shift is bigger.
reading: Real events often push both curves at the same time. Take the worst week of the summer on Maple Street: the heat wave hits and the price of lemons doubles in the same week. Demand shifts right, which pushes price up and quantity up. Supply shifts left, which pushes price up and quantity down. Both shifts push the price up, so the price definitely rises. But one shift pushes quantity up and the other pushes it down. Quantity could go either way.

Which way quantity goes depends on which shift is bigger. If the heat wave is huge and the lemon price rise is small, the demand shift wins and quantity rises. If the heat is mild and lemons are suddenly unaffordable, the supply shift wins and quantity falls. Without knowing the sizes, an economist says quantity is *indeterminate*: it cannot be determined from the directions alone. That is an honest answer, not a dodge.

There are four two-curve combinations. Demand right and supply left: price up for sure, quantity uncertain. Demand left and supply right: price down for sure, quantity uncertain. Demand right and supply right: quantity up for sure, price uncertain. Demand left and supply left: quantity down for sure, price uncertain. In every case, one variable is certain because both shifts agree on it, and the other is uncertain because they disagree.

The spring of 2020 was a giant version of this. Demand for many things like restaurant meals and airline seats shifted sharply left. At the same time, supply of many goods shifted left as factories and ports slowed. For some products prices rose, for others they fell, depending on which curve moved more. When the news seems contradictory, sort each event into its curve and direction. The contradictions usually turn out to be two shifts at once.

words.d: cannot be decided from the information given; used when two shifts push a variable in opposite directions
when the demand curve and the supply curve move in the same period
which of two shifts is larger; it decides the uncertain variable when both curves move

look.title: Sort the Double Shift
look.text: A new soybean-processing plant opens in central Illinois and buys far more soybeans than before (a shifter on the buyers' side). The same year, excellent weather gives farmers a record harvest (a shifter on the sellers' side).
look.prompt: Name each shift and its direction. Which of price and quantity is certain, and which is indeterminate? What extra information would settle the uncertain one?

check.q: Demand shifts right and supply shifts left at the same time. What do we know for sure?
check.why: Both shifts push price up. They push quantity in opposite directions, so quantity is indeterminate.

check.q: Demand and supply both shift right. Which is certain?
check.why: Both shifts raise quantity. One raises price and the other lowers it, so price is indeterminate.

check.q: What does it mean when an economist says the change in quantity is indeterminate?
choices: The two shifts push quantity opposite ways and the sizes are unknown
check.why: Indeterminate means the direction cannot be decided from the shift directions alone; the relative sizes would settle it.

lessons.title: Measuring the Response
lessons.mainIdea: Price elasticity of demand is the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in price.
reading: The law of demand says buyers buy less when the price rises. It does not say how much less. That is what *elasticity* measures. Maya raises her lemonade from $1.00 to $1.20. That is a 20% price increase, because 0.20 divided by 1.00 is 0.20. Her sales fall from 40 cups to 30 cups an hour, a 25% drop, because 10 divided by 40 is 0.25. The *price elasticity of demand* is the percent change in quantity divided by the percent change in price: 25% divided by 20% equals 1.25.

Read that number as "quantity moved 1.25 times as much as price did, in percent." Economists drop the minus sign, since quantity and price always move opposite ways for demand. When the number is greater than 1, demand is *elastic*: buyers respond strongly, like a stretchy rubber band. When it is less than 1, demand is *inelastic*: buyers barely budge. When it is exactly 1, demand is unit elastic.

Now try gas. A station raises its price from $3.00 to $3.60 a gallon, a 20% increase. Deshawn's dad still has to drive to work, so he cuts back from 10 gallons a week to 9.5, a 5% drop. Elasticity is 5% divided by 20%, which is 0.25. Inelastic. The same 20% price rise that cost Maya a quarter of her customers cost the gas station almost none of its gallons.

Two warnings. First, elasticity uses percents, not raw amounts, so you can compare lemonade cups with gallons of gas. Second, this is the simple method used in introductory classes. Economists often use a midpoint formula that gives the same answer whether the price goes up or down. Your teacher will tell you which to use. Either way, the meaning is the same: a big number means buyers are sensitive to price, and a small number means they are not.

words.d: a measure of how strongly one quantity responds to a change in another, in percent terms
percent change in quantity demanded divided by percent change in price
elasticity greater than 1; quantity changes by a larger percent than price
elasticity less than 1; quantity changes by a smaller percent than price

look.title: Same Price Rise, Different Responses
look.cite: Illustrative values built for this lesson.
look.prompt: Which goods are elastic and which are inelastic? For each, name the reason you think buyers respond that much or that little.

check.q: Price rises 20% and quantity demanded falls 25%. What is the elasticity of demand?
check.why: Elasticity is 25% divided by 20%, which is 1.25. Quantity moved 1.25 times as much as price.

check.q: Gas rises from $3.00 to $3.60 and a driver cuts from 10 gallons to 9.5. What is the elasticity?
check.why: Price rose 20% (0.60 ÷ 3.00). Quantity fell 5% (0.5 ÷ 10). Elasticity is 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25.

check.q: An elasticity of 0.25 means demand is
choices: inelastic: buyers barely change their quantity when price changes
elastic: buyers respond strongly to price
impossible, since elasticity must be above 1
check.why: Below 1 is inelastic. Quantity changed by a smaller percent than price did.

lessons.title: What Makes Demand Elastic
lessons.mainIdea: Demand is more elastic when a good has close substitutes, takes a big share of the budget, is a luxury rather than a necessity, and when buyers have time to adjust.
reading: Why did lemonade buyers flee a 20% price rise while gas buyers barely noticed? Four things decide how elastic demand is. The first and biggest is *substitutes*. Lemonade has many: iced tea, water, soda, juice. When the price rises, buyers have somewhere to go. Gas, for someone who has to drive to work, has almost none in the short run. The more and closer the substitutes, the more elastic the demand. That is also why the demand for one brand of gas is elastic even though the demand for gas in general is not.

The second is *share of budget*. A 20% rise in the price of table salt costs a family a few cents a year, so nobody changes anything. A 20% rise in rent might be $200 a month, so families move, get roommates, or look farther from the city. Goods that take a big slice of income tend to have more elastic demand, because a price change there really hurts and buyers respond.

The third is *necessity versus luxury*. Insulin for someone with diabetes is a necessity and its demand is very inelastic. A weekend at a water park is a luxury; if the price doubles, most families skip it. Note that necessity is about the buyer's situation, not the product's dignity. Gas is a necessity for a commuter with no bus line and a luxury for someone who mostly bikes.

The fourth is *time*. Right after gas prices jump, drivers can do little, so demand is inelastic. Over a year, they can carpool, buy a more efficient car, move closer to work, or take the train. Demand becomes more elastic the longer buyers have to adjust. When you estimate elasticity, always ask: elastic over what time period? The answer for the same good can be 0.2 in a month and close to 1 over several years.

words.d: other goods that do a similar job; more and closer substitutes make demand more elastic
how much of a buyer's income a good takes; a larger share makes demand more elastic
a good the buyer feels they cannot do without; its demand tends to be inelastic
a good the buyer can easily skip; its demand tends to be elastic

look.title: Rank the Four
look.text: Four goods: a specific brand of bottled water; electricity for your home; a $1,200 vacation to Florida; and a prescription medicine with no generic version. Each one's price rises by 25%.
look.prompt: Rank the four from most elastic to least elastic demand. For each, name the factor (substitutes, budget share, necessity, or time) that most drove your ranking.

check.q: Which good most likely has the MOST elastic demand?
choices: One brand of bottled water among many
Gasoline in the first week after a price rise
check.why: A single brand has many close substitutes (every other brand), so buyers switch easily. That makes demand elastic.

check.q: Why does demand for gas become more elastic over several years than over one month?
choices: Because prices always fall over time
Because buyers have time to find substitutes, like a more efficient car or a train
Because the share of budget rises
check.why: Time lets buyers adjust. With more options available, quantity responds more to price.

check.q: Table salt's price rises 30% and sales barely change. Which factor best explains this?
choices: Buyers have had lots of time
Salt takes a tiny share of the budget
check.why: A price rise on something that costs almost nothing per year is not worth changing behavior over, so demand is inelastic.

lessons.title: Elasticity and Total Revenue
lessons.mainIdea: Raising the price lowers total revenue when demand is elastic and raises it when demand is inelastic.
reading: A seller thinking about a price change wants to know one thing: will I take in more money or less? *Total revenue* is price times quantity sold. Maya at $1.00 sold 40 cups, so her total revenue was $40. At $1.20 she sold 30 cups, for $36. She raised her price and took in less money. That happened because her demand was elastic (1.25). Buyers left faster, in percent, than the price rose, so the lost sales outweighed the higher price per cup.

The gas station had the opposite experience. At $3.00 Deshawn's dad bought 10 gallons a week: $30. At $3.60 he bought 9.5 gallons: $34.20. Revenue rose. With inelastic demand (0.25), the price rise gained more than the tiny drop in gallons lost. The rule: when demand is elastic, price and total revenue move in opposite directions. When demand is inelastic, price and total revenue move in the same direction. When demand is unit elastic, revenue barely changes.

Look at a small concert venue that seats 100 and is testing prices. At $5 it sells 100 tickets for $500. At $10, 80 tickets for $800. At $15, 60 tickets for $900. At $20, 40 tickets for $800. At $25, 20 tickets for $500. Revenue rises as the price climbs from $5 to $15, so demand is inelastic in that range. Revenue falls from $15 to $25, so demand is elastic there. Along one straight demand curve, elasticity changes: inelastic at low prices, elastic at high prices.

This is the *revenue test*, and businesses use it constantly. A streaming service raising its monthly fee is betting demand is inelastic. A restaurant running a half-price Tuesday is betting demand that night is elastic. Neither needs the formula. If revenue goes up after a price increase, demand was inelastic. If it goes down, demand was elastic. The formula and the revenue test always agree.

words.d: the money a seller takes in: price times quantity sold
if a price rise raises total revenue, demand is inelastic; if it lowers total revenue, demand is elastic
elasticity equal to 1; a price change leaves total revenue roughly unchanged

look.title: Ticket Price and Total Revenue
look.cite: A labeled example built for this lesson; not a real venue.
look.prompt: Over which price range is demand inelastic? Elastic? If the venue's only goal were the most revenue, which price should it choose?

check.q: Maya raises her price from $1.00 to $1.20 and sales fall from 40 to 30 cups. What happened to her total revenue?
check.why: Revenue is price times quantity: 40 × $1.00 = $40, then 30 × $1.20 = $36. Elastic demand means revenue fell.

check.q: A company raises its price 10% and its total revenue goes up. What does the revenue test say?
check.why: When price and revenue move in the same direction, quantity fell by a smaller percent than price rose. That is inelastic demand.

check.q: In the ticket table, revenue is $800 at $20 and $500 at $25. Demand between those prices is
check.why: Price rose and revenue fell, so quantity dropped by a larger percent than price rose. That is elastic demand.

lessons.title: Elasticity of Supply
lessons.mainIdea: Price elasticity of supply measures how much sellers change quantity supplied when the price changes, and it depends mostly on time.
reading: Sellers have an elasticity too. *Price elasticity of supply* is the percent change in quantity supplied divided by the percent change in price. When lemonade rose from $1.00 to $1.50, a 50% increase, Deshawn's cups rose from 30 to 45, also a 50% increase. His elasticity of supply was 50% divided by 50%, which is 1.0. The same labels apply: above 1 is elastic, below 1 is inelastic.

What decides it? Mostly how easily sellers can make more, and that depends on *time*. A Van Gogh painting has an elasticity of supply of zero: raise the price all you want and there will never be another. Economists call that *perfectly inelastic*. Arena seats for one night are almost the same: 18,000 exist, and the price cannot change that number this week. Over a year, though, the promoter could add a second night, so supply becomes more elastic when the time period is longer.

Illinois corn shows the same pattern. In the middle of the growing season, a price jump changes almost nothing; the seeds are already in the ground. By next spring, farmers can plant more acres of corn and fewer of soybeans, so the yearly quantity responds a good deal. Across several years, new land can be rented and new equipment bought. The longer the time, the more elastic the supply.

Elasticity of supply also depends on whether inputs are easy to get. Lemonade is elastic because lemons, sugar and cups are easy to buy more of. A restaurant that needs a licensed chef, a kitchen and a permit cannot double its meals overnight. Goods that need scarce or slow-to-build inputs have inelastic supply. When you see a price spike that lasts, it usually means supply could not respond quickly.

words.d: percent change in quantity supplied divided by percent change in price
an elasticity of zero; quantity does not change at all when price changes
how long sellers or buyers have to adjust; longer periods make both supply and demand more elastic

look.title: Fixed Tonight, Flexible Next Year
look.text: Hotel rooms near the arena on concert night are all booked by the afternoon, and the price on booking sites doubles. Nobody can build a hotel by tonight. Over the next three years, two new hotels open two blocks away.
look.prompt: Describe the elasticity of supply for hotel rooms on concert night versus over three years. What does that difference do to how long the high price lasts?

check.q: Price rises 50% and quantity supplied rises 50%. Elasticity of supply is
check.why: 50% divided by 50% equals 1.0, unit elastic.

check.q: Why is the supply of arena seats for tonight's concert almost perfectly inelastic?
choices: Because the number of seats cannot change no matter what the price is
Because fans do not care about price
Because the arena is a necessity
check.why: Perfectly inelastic supply means quantity is fixed. Nothing about tonight's price can add seats.

check.q: Why is supply of corn more elastic over three years than during one growing season?
choices: Because demand for corn is elastic
Because farmers can plant more acres and buy equipment given time
check.why: Time lets sellers adjust inputs. During a season the crop is already planted; across years, acres and equipment can change.

lessons.title: Elasticity in Everyday Decisions
lessons.mainIdea: Knowing whether demand is elastic or inelastic predicts how buyers, sellers and governments will fare when a price changes.
reading: Elasticity is not just a number for tests. Imagine you run a small bakery in Peoria and your flour costs jump. Should you raise your bread price by 10% or eat the cost? If your bread is much like the bread at three other bakeries nearby, demand is elastic, and a 10% rise might cost you 20% of your customers and cut revenue. If you are the only bakery for miles and people love your bread, demand is inelastic, and the price rise mostly sticks. The right choice depends on the elasticity.

Governments use the same reasoning. A tax on cigarettes raises a lot of money precisely because demand for cigarettes is inelastic: people keep buying even when the price rises, so the tax collects steadily. The same inelasticity means the tax does less to cut smoking than its supporters hope, at least in the short run. A tax on a good with elastic demand does the opposite: it cuts sales a lot and collects little. Economists point this out whichever goal a lawmaker has.

Elasticity also explains why some price spikes hurt more than others. When gas rises 20%, families cannot cut back much, so their weekly bill really goes up. When strawberries rise 20%, families buy blueberries or skip fruit that week, and the bill barely moves. Inelastic goods are the ones where a price rise lands on the *consumer* and stays there. Elastic goods are the ones where a price rise is mostly the seller's problem.

Finally, elasticity is a prediction tool for the two-curve stories in this chapter. When supply shifts left, how much the price rises depends on how elastic demand is. If demand is inelastic, like gas, a small supply cut causes a big price jump because buyers will not back off. If demand is elastic, like one brand of soda, the same supply cut barely moves the price because buyers walk away. This is why gasoline prices swing so wildly while soda prices do not.

words.d: a person who buys goods or services for their own use
the money a government collects from a tax; larger when demand for the taxed good is inelastic
a sudden, large rise in a price, often when supply shifts left and demand is inelastic

look.title: The Bakery's Choice
look.text: A Peoria bakery sells 500 loaves a week at $4.00, for $2,000 in revenue. Flour costs jump. The owner estimates that at $4.40 she would sell 440 loaves if demand is fairly inelastic, or 380 loaves if demand is elastic, depending on how loyal her customers are.
look.prompt: Compute revenue in each case. In which case does the price rise pay off? What could the owner do to learn which case she is in before committing?

check.q: A bakery raises its price 10% and, because three similar bakeries are nearby, loses 20% of its sales. This tells you demand was
check.why: Quantity fell by a larger percent (20%) than price rose (10%), so elasticity is 2. Elastic demand means revenue fell.

check.q: Why does a tax on cigarettes raise a lot of money?
choices: Because demand for cigarettes is inelastic, so people keep buying
Because the tax shifts demand right
check.why: With inelastic demand, a higher price barely reduces quantity, so the tax collects on almost as many units as before.

check.q: Supply of gas and supply of one brand of soda both shift left by the same amount. Which price rises more, and why?
choices: Soda, because it is a luxury
Both rise equally, since the shift is the same
Gas, because demand for gas is inelastic and buyers do not back off
Soda, because it has inelastic demand
check.why: With inelastic demand, buyers keep buying as the price climbs, so a supply cut produces a big price rise.

lessons.title: The Ticket Puzzle Solved
lessons.mainIdea: A concert ticket priced below equilibrium with a fixed supply creates a shortage, and the resale market is where the price rises to clear it.
reading: Now put the whole chapter on Jada's ticket. Supply: 18,000 seats, perfectly inelastic for that night. Demand: about 60,000 fans at $75, about 18,000 at $250. The equilibrium price is around $250, because that is where the quantity fans want equals the seats that exist. The artist charged $75, far below equilibrium. At $75 the shortage was about 42,000. Something other than price had to decide who got in, and on Friday morning that was the online queue.

Why would an artist leave so much money on the table? There are real reasons. Some want younger fans and less wealthy fans to have a chance, and a low *face value* plus a random queue does that better than a $250 price. Some fear the bad press of being called greedy. Some want a guaranteed sellout and a full, loud room. These are choices about who gets the seats, and they are legitimate. But the shortage they create does not go away. It moves.

It moves to the *resale market*, where the price is free. Sellers who got tickets at $75 offer them at $220, $340 or $900, and buyers who value the show most, or simply have the most money, take them. Elasticity explains the size of the jump. Supply is fixed, so it cannot respond at all. Demand for one specific singer on one specific night has few substitutes and is fairly inelastic, so it takes a very high price to trim 60,000 eager fans down to 18,000 seats. A four-times markup is what that looks like.

Compare milk. If a grocery store sold milk at half the going price, it would run out, but nobody would resell milk at four times the price, because the store down the street has plenty and supply is elastic. The ticket story is dramatic because both curves are extreme: perfectly inelastic supply and inelastic demand. Whether resale should be limited, or whether artists should just charge more, is a debate with good arguments on both sides. The economics tells you what will happen either way. It does not tell you what is fair.

words.d: the price printed on a ticket, set by the seller; it may be above or below the equilibrium price
a market where people who already bought a good sell it again, usually at whatever price buyers will pay
a price set lower than the market-clearing price; it creates a shortage and non-price rationing

look.title: Two Ways to Sell 18,000 Seats
look.text: Plan A: charge $75, let the online queue decide, and accept a large resale market. Plan B: charge $250, so the market clears and there is little resale, and give 2,000 free tickets by lottery to students. Assume the same 60,000 fans want to go at $75 and 18,000 at $250.
look.prompt: For each plan, who ends up with seats and how much money goes to the artist versus resellers? Which plan would you choose, and what trade-off are you accepting?

check.q: Fans want 60,000 tickets at $75 and there are 18,000 seats. Which statement is correct?
choices: The price of $75 is the equilibrium price
There is a shortage of 42,000 at $75
check.why: Shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 60,000 minus 18,000 equals 42,000. The price is below equilibrium.

check.q: Why does resale drive the ticket price up so much more than a shortage of milk ever would?
choices: Because ticket supply is fixed and demand for that show has few substitutes
Because milk is a normal good
Because ticket sellers are greedier than grocers
Because demand for tickets is elastic
check.why: Perfectly inelastic supply plus inelastic demand means a very high price is needed to reduce quantity demanded to the fixed number of seats.

check.q: An artist sets a face value below equilibrium so that younger fans have a chance. Which result should the artist expect?
choices: The shortage disappears because the price is fair
Non-price rationing, such as a queue, and a resale market with higher prices
Supply of seats will rise to meet demand
check.why: A below-equilibrium price leaves a shortage. Something else rations the seats, and resale lets the price rise toward equilibrium.

review.q: At $6 buyers want 90 units and sellers offer 90. At $5 buyers want 110 and sellers offer 70. What is true at $5?
choices: A shortage of 40 units, and the price will rise
A surplus of 40 units, and the price will fall
review.why: At $5, quantity demanded (110) exceeds quantity supplied (70) by 40. That shortage pushes the price up toward $6.

review.q: A new study says walnuts are good for the heart, and walnut prices and sales both rise. Which shift explains this?
review.why: Price and quantity rose together, which only a rightward demand shift produces. Tastes changed.

review.q: A drought cuts the wheat harvest. What happens to the price and quantity of bread?
review.why: Higher input costs shift the supply of bread left. Price rises and quantity sold falls.

review.q: Demand shifts left and supply shifts left at the same time. Which is certain?
review.why: Both shifts reduce quantity. One lowers price and the other raises it, so price is indeterminate.

review.q: A price rises from $20 to $25 and quantity demanded falls from 200 to 150. What is the elasticity of demand?
review.why: Price rose 25% (5 ÷ 20). Quantity fell 25% (50 ÷ 200). Elasticity is 25 ÷ 25 = 1.0.

review.q: Which good is likely to have the most inelastic demand?
choices: One brand of chips among dozens
A prescription drug with no substitute
A weekend at a theme park
review.why: A necessity with no substitutes leaves buyers no way to respond to a higher price.

review.q: A café raises its coffee price and its total revenue falls. The revenue test says demand for its coffee is
review.why: When price rises and revenue falls, quantity fell by a larger percent than price rose. That is elastic demand.

review.q: Why is the supply of seats for a concert tonight almost perfectly inelastic?
choices: The number of seats cannot change in response to price
review.why: Perfectly inelastic supply means quantity is fixed no matter what the price is. Seats cannot be added by tonight.
